scores.evidence: Tag images with the git commit and promote that exact image through every environment. Never rebuild per environment.
scores.rationale: Mechanisms (OIDC, expand/contract, GitOps rollback, admission audit mode) are correct; the runner concurrency math (~50 at once) is loose but minor, and git-tag immutability isn't enforced explicitly.

scores.evidence: Sort them into 4–6 types... you build about 5 shared pipeline templates instead of 50 separate pipelines.
scores.rationale: Covers the sequencing request well with pilot, waves and explicit deferrals, though test environments and runner buy/build are thin.

scores.evidence: Main sequence: decisions → runners, registry, access and GitOps → pilot in production → versioned templates → Wave 1 → 2 → 3.
scores.rationale: Consistent design with clear dependencies; minor loose ends such as a pilot in production before templates and overlapping phase timings.

scores.evidence: the pilot has shipped through the platform for 2+ weeks, a rollback drill has passed, and lead time has been compared with the baseline.
scores.rationale: Risky assumptions are validated early with checkable gates and a DORA baseline, but criteria like the change failure threshold are left unspecified.

scores.evidence: the services are (or will be) in containers on Kubernetes, code is on GitHub or GitLab, and a platform team of 4–6 people
scores.rationale: Key assumptions are stated with a note on timing sensitivity; the runner volume figures are illustrative, and compliance and budget are not covered.

scores.evidence: One careless change to an unversioned template can break all 50 pipelines at once.
scores.rationale: Covers template blast radius, migration stalls, vulnerability-block workarounds and rollback, but omits CI outage plans, fork/untrusted PR handling, and flaky-test detail.

scores.evidence: Build everything as infrastructure-as-code, and give the platform its own pipeline from day one.
scores.rationale: Deployment, rollback drills, migrations, monitoring and support model are concrete; the platform owner and on-call/outage plan are not named.

scores.evidence: 50 services × ~15 runs a day × ~10 minutes, with 3× peaks during working hours
scores.rationale: Runner sizing has a basis, but there's no dollar estimate, hosted vs self-hosted choice, or concrete cost controls beyond retention and a mention of PR environments.

scores.evidence: Write down the decisions that are expensive to reverse... Leave easy-to-change choices, like which scanner to buy, for later.
scores.rationale: Order is explicitly driven by reversibility, with hard-to-undo decisions first, versioned templates, and reversible choices deferred.

scores.evidence: Add a developer portal only after the standard path is proven.
scores.rationale: Proportionate, with deferral of portal, PR environments and enforcement; GitOps, admission control and 8 months are mild overhead but justified.

scores.evidence: it uses a pinned template version, deploys through GitOps to every environment, ships a signed image... and its old pipeline is deleted.
scores.rationale: Ordered by dependencies with done-when criteria, wave definitions and prerequisites per step; tool choice and backlog left open.

checklist.evidence: you build about 5 shared pipeline templates instead of 50 separate pipelines... extension points so unusual cases don't need their own copies
run the old and new pipelines side by side briefly, then switch.
Tag images with the git commit and promote that exact image through every environment. Never rebuild per environment.
CI signing into the cloud with short-lived tokens (OIDC) instead of stored keys.
software bill of materials → sign → push... only signed images from your registry
Database migrations run before each deploy using expand/contract... a rollback you've actually practiced.
Contract tests (e.g., Pact) check that services still agree on their APIs. They let services deploy independently.
Temporary environments per pull request, but only where they're worth the cost... Quarantine flaky tests
CI duration under 10–15 minutes... runners... cache builds
Size them for peak load... 50 services × ~15 runs a day × ~10 minutes, with 3× peaks
Targets for the platform itself: availability, queue time... DORA metrics per service
Keep a manual production approval for now... Single sign-on, role-based access and audit logs.

traps.evidence: Wave 1 (~7)... End each wave by deleting the old pipelines by a fixed date.
no `:latest` tags... Never rebuild per environment.
short-lived tokens (OIDC) instead of stored keys.
Contract tests... let services deploy independently. Keep full end-to-end tests to a small set

note: Strong sequencing plan with good reversibility and migration reasoning; thinner on runner cost, untrusted PR handling, test environments and platform ownership and outage planning.
